claim: Many decisions are thought to arise via the accumulation of noisy evidence to a threshold or bound.
source: Many decisions are thought to arise via the accumulation of noisy evidence to a threshold or bound.
evidence: This is a statement of established theory in the field, supported by the broader literature context.

claim: The bounded accumulation mechanism explains the effect of stimulus strength, characterized by signal-to-noise ratio, on decision speed, accuracy and confidence.
source: In perception, the mechanism explains the effect of stimulus strength, characterized by signal-to-noise ratio, on decision speed, accuracy and confidence.
evidence: This is a statement about what the theoretical mechanism explains, based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: An increase in noise should lead to faster decisions.
source: An increase in noise should lead to faster decisions, reduced accuracy and, paradoxically, higher confidence.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction derived from the bounded accumulation model.

claim: An increase in noise should lead to reduced accuracy.
source: An increase in noise should lead to faster decisions, reduced accuracy and, paradoxically, higher confidence.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction derived from the bounded accumulation model.

claim: An increase in noise should lead to higher confidence.
source: An increase in noise should lead to faster decisions, reduced accuracy and, paradoxically, higher confidence.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction derived from the bounded accumulation model.

claim: A novel sensory manipulation mimics the addition of unbiased noise to motion-selective regions of visual cortex.
source: To test these predictions, we introduce a novel sensory manipulation that mimics the addition of unbiased noise to motion-selective regions of visual cortex, which we verified with neuronal recordings from macaque areas MT/MST.
evidence: This claim is supported by neuronal recordings from macaque areas MT/MST as stated in the text.

claim: The volatility manipulation was verified with neuronal recordings from macaque areas MT/MST.
source: To test these predictions, we introduce a novel sensory manipulation that mimics the addition of unbiased noise to motion-selective regions of visual cortex, which we verified with neuronal recordings from macaque areas MT/MST.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by the neurophysiological data presented in the manuscript.

claim: For both humans and monkeys, increasing the noise induced faster decisions.
source: For both humans and monkeys, increasing the noise induced faster decisions and greater confidence over a range of stimuli for which accuracy was minimally impaired.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from both species.

claim: For both humans and monkeys, increasing the noise induced greater confidence.
source: For both humans and monkeys, increasing the noise induced faster decisions and greater confidence over a range of stimuli for which accuracy was minimally impaired.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from both species.

claim: Increasing the noise minimally impaired accuracy over a range of stimuli.
source: For both humans and monkeys, increasing the noise induced faster decisions and greater confidence over a range of stimuli for which accuracy was minimally impaired.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The magnitude of the effects was in agreement with predictions of a bounded evidence accumulation model.
source: The magnitude of the effects was in agreement with predictions of a bounded evidence accumulation model.
evidence: This is supported by the model fits to the data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Decisions that combine information from different sources or across time serve as a model of cognitive function.
source: Decisions that combine information from different sources or across time are of special interest to neuroscience because they serve as a model of cognitive function.
evidence: This is a statement about the conceptual framework of the field.

claim: These decisions are not hard wired or reflexive, yet they are experimentally tractable.
source: These decisions are not hard wired or reflexive, yet they are experimentally tractable.
evidence: This is a characterization of the type of decisions studied, based on established knowledge.

claim: RT furnishes a powerful constraint on models of decision-making.
source: RT furnishes a powerful constraint on models of decision-making, and is a defining element of the trade-off between speed and accuracy that characterizes most decisions.
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical importance of RT in decision-making research.

claim: RT is a defining element of the trade-off between speed and accuracy that characterizes most decisions.
source: RT furnishes a powerful constraint on models of decision-making, and is a defining element of the trade-off between speed and accuracy that characterizes most decisions.
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical importance of RT in decision-making research.

claim: Decision confidence influences how we learn from our mistakes.
source: This belief, referred to as decision confidence, influences many aspects of behavior: how we learn from our mistakes, plan subsequent decisions, and communicate our decisions to others.
evidence: This is a statement about the role of confidence in behavior, based on established knowledge.

claim: Decision confidence influences how we plan subsequent decisions.
source: This belief, referred to as decision confidence, influences many aspects of behavior: how we learn from our mistakes, plan subsequent decisions, and communicate our decisions to others.
evidence: This is a statement about the role of confidence in behavior, based on established knowledge.

claim: Decision confidence influences how we communicate our decisions to others.
source: This belief, referred to as decision confidence, influences many aspects of behavior: how we learn from our mistakes, plan subsequent decisions, and communicate our decisions to others.
evidence: This is a statement about the role of confidence in behavior, based on established knowledge.

claim: The family of bounded evidence accumulation models offers a framework for linking choice, reaction time and confidence.
source: The family of bounded evidence accumulation models, including drift diffusion, race and attractor models, offers one such framework for linking choice, reaction time and confidence [for reviews, see Gold and Shadlen (2007); Shadlen and Kiani (2013)].
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Bounded accumulation models depict the decision process as a race between competing accumulators.
source: These models depict the decision process as a race between competing accumulators, each of which integrates momentary evidence for one alternative and against the others.
evidence: This is a description of the theoretical framework.

claim: The decision terminates when the accumulated evidence for one alternative reaches a threshold or bound.
source: The decision terminates when the accumulated evidence for one alternative, termed a decision variable (DV), reaches a threshold or bound, thereby determining both the choice and the decision time.
evidence: This is a description of the theoretical framework.

claim: Confidence in the decision derives from a mapping between the DV and the probability that a decision based on this DV will be correct.
source: Confidence in the decision derives from a mapping between the DV and the probability that a decision based on this DV will be correct.
evidence: This is a description of how confidence is conceptualized in the theoretical framework.

claim: The mapping between DV and confidence is thought to incorporate the decision time or the state of the competing (losing) accumulator(s), or both.
source: The mapping is thought to incorporate the decision time or the state of the competing (losing) accumulator(s), or both (Vickers, 1979; Kiani and Shadlen, 2009; Zylberberg et al., 2012; Kiani et al., 2014; Van den Berg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Trial to trial variation in the activity of neurons in MT/MST were indicative of the choice that the monkey was about to make.
source: Consistent with earlier reports (Britten et al., 1992), trial to trial variation in the activity of neurons in MT/MST were indicative of the choice that the monkey was about to make.
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 7A and cited prior work.

claim: The fluctuations in neural activity were more informative in the high volatility condition.
source: The fluctuations were more informative in the high volatility condition, presumably because they were induced by exaggerated variance in the motion display itself (e.g., Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the neural data analysis and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: The time course of choice-related signals evolved with similar latencies in the low and high volatility conditions.
source: Notably, the time course of choice-related signals evolved with similar latencies in the low and high volatility conditions.
evidence: This is supported by the latency analysis of neural data.

claim: The latencies of choice-related signals were comparable to that of the direction selective signal itself.
source: The latencies were comparable to that of the direction selective signal itself (Figure 7B), suggesting that the choice was informed by the earliest motion information available in the stimulus (Kiani et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7B and cited prior work.

claim: The choice was informed by the earliest motion information available in the stimulus.
source: The latencies were comparable to that of the direction selective signal itself (Figure 7B), suggesting that the choice was informed by the earliest motion information available in the stimulus (Kiani et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference supported by the neural data and cited prior work.

claim: The trial-by-trial variation in neural activity was correlated with the decision to accept or waive the sure-bet option.
source: The trial-by-trial variation in neural activity was also correlated with the decision to accept or waive the sure-bet option, when it was offered.
evidence: This is supported by the neural data analysis presented in Figure 7C-D.

claim: Early motion evidence simultaneously informs both choice and confidence.
source: These results indicate that early motion evidence simultaneously informs both choice and confidence (Zylberberg et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the neural data analysis and cited prior work.

claim: The results are inconsistent with the proposal that choice and confidence are resolved in strict succession.
source: They are inconsistent with the proposal that choice and confidence are resolved in strict succession, as these predict that confidence selectivity ought to emerge later than choice-related signals (Pleskac and Busemeyer, 2010; Navajas et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference from the data that contradicts predictions from cited alternative models.

claim: A stimulus manipulation that increases the variance of the momentary evidence increases both the speed of the decision and the confidence associated with it.
source: We have shown that a stimulus manipulation that increases the variance of the momentary evidence bearing on a decision—what we term volatility—increases both the speed of the decision and the confidence associated with it.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The approach differs from recent studies in that it applied the manipulation to a well studied motion task for which much is known about the underlying physiology.
source: Our approach differs from recent studies that have attempted to vary evidence reliability through stimulus manipulations (de Gardelle and Summerfield, 2011; Zylberberg et al., 2014; de Gardelle and Mamassian, 2015) in that we (i) applied the manipulation to a well studied motion task for which much is known about the underlying physiology
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological approach, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The approach differs from recent studies in that it verified the effect of the manipulation by recording from neurons in the visual cortex of the macaque.
source: Our approach differs from recent studies that have attempted to vary evidence reliability through stimulus manipulations (de Gardelle and Summerfield, 2011; Zylberberg et al., 2014; de Gardelle and Mamassian, 2015) in that we (i) applied the manipulation to a well studied motion task for which much is known about the underlying physiology; (ii) verified the effect of the manipulation by recording from neurons in the visual cortex of the macaque
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological approach, supported by the neurophysiological data.

claim: The approach showed how a framework based on the bounded accumulation of evidence can account for the joint effect of volatility on choice, reaction time and confidence.
source: Our approach differs from recent studies that have attempted to vary evidence reliability through stimulus manipulations (de Gardelle and Summerfield, 2011; Zylberberg et al., 2014; de Gardelle and Mamassian, 2015) in that we (i) applied the manipulation to a well studied motion task for which much is known about the underlying physiology; (ii) verified the effect of the manipulation by recording from neurons in the visual cortex of the macaque, and (iii) showed how a framework based on the bounded accumulation of evidence can account for the joint effect of volatility on choice, reaction time and confidence.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The modeling framework was able to explain the observed pattern of choices, RTs and confidence in a quantitatively coherent way.
source: The modeling framework pursued here was able to explain the observed pattern of choices, RTs and confidence in a quantitatively coherent way (Figures 3–5), even predicting subjects' confidence ratings (Figure 5B) based on a fit to their RT data from a separate experiment (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the model fits shown in Figures 3-5.

claim: The model predicted subjects' confidence ratings based on a fit to their RT data from a separate experiment.
source: The modeling framework pursued here was able to explain the observed pattern of choices, RTs and confidence in a quantitatively coherent way (Figures 3–5), even predicting subjects' confidence ratings (Figure 5B) based on a fit to their RT data from a separate experiment (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the model predictions shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Increased volatility disperses the decision variable away from its expectation.
source: The intuition is that increased volatility disperses the decision variable away from its expectation.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism underlying the observed effects.

claim: For low coherences, increased volatility accelerates departure from the starting point and closer to one of the decision bounds.
source: For low coherences, it accelerates departure from the starting point (i.e., neutral evidence) and closer to one of the decision bounds.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism underlying the observed effects.

claim: The tendency to arrive at larger absolute values of accumulated evidence leads to faster and more confident decisions.
source: This tendency to arrive at larger absolute values of accumulated evidence—in support of either choice—leads to faster and more confident decisions (Zylberberg et al., 2012; Maniscalco et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an explanation supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Subjects do not change their decision strategy based on the volatility of the evidence on a particular trial.
source: These intuitions and our fits to the data rest on the assumption that subjects do not change their decision strategy based on the volatility of the evidence on a particular trial.
evidence: This is an assumption of the modeling approach, tested against alternative models.

claim: Subjects applied the same termination policy (i.e., decision bound) for both volatility conditions.
source: On all trials, we assumed subjects applied the same termination policy (i.e., decision bound) and the same mapping between the state of the evidence and confidence, for both volatility conditions as well as for all motion strengths (Gorea and Sagi, 2000; Kiani and Shadlen, 2009).
evidence: This is an assumption of the modeling approach, supported by citations and model comparisons.

claim: Subjects applied the same mapping between the state of the evidence and confidence for both volatility conditions.
source: On all trials, we assumed subjects applied the same termination policy (i.e., decision bound) and the same mapping between the state of the evidence and confidence, for both volatility conditions as well as for all motion strengths (Gorea and Sagi, 2000; Kiani and Shadlen, 2009).
evidence: This is an assumption of the modeling approach, supported by citations and model comparisons.

claim: Alternative models in which the brain uses volatility to adjust the mapping and/or the decision bound were rejected.
source: We considered and rejected alternative models in which the brain uses volatility to adjust the mapping and/or the decision bound.
evidence: This is supported by the model comparison analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: If different mappings between DV and confidence were used for the low and high volatility conditions, a larger excursion of the DV would be required in the high volatility condition to reach the same level of confidence.
source: In particular, if different mappings between DV and confidence were used for the low and high volatility conditions, a larger excursion of the DV would be required in the high volatility condition to reach the same level of confidence, predicting a pattern of post-decision wagering behavior that was not supported by our data (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a prediction from an alternative model that was not supported by the data.

claim: The normative solution for a simplified version of the RT task is to increase the bound height on high volatility trials.
source: Indeed, the normative solution for a simplified version of the RT task is to increase the bound height on high volatility trials, which nevertheless leads to slightly faster responses than for low volatility trials when the motion is weak (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This is a theoretical result from a normative analysis.

claim: Models that posit an online estimation of reliability make predictions that run counter to one or more of the trends observed in the data.
source: Thus, models that posit an online estimation of reliability [cf., Deneve (2012); Yeung and Summerfield (2012); Qamar et al. (2013)] make predictions that run counter to one or more of the trends we observed.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing model predictions to the observed data.

claim: The experiment is representative of a broad class of decisions for which the reliability of the evidence is unknown to the decision-maker before beginning deliberation.
source: However, our experiment—in particular, the mixture of interleaved motion strengths and the volatility manipulation—is representative of a broad class of decisions for which the reliability of the evidence is unknown to the decision-maker before beginning deliberation and not readily apparent from a small number of samples.
evidence: This is a characterization of the experimental design and its implications.

claim: In a detection task where the stimulus categories were signaled by an external cue, human subjects did not adjust the decision criterion to the levels used when each stimulus category was presented on its own.
source: In a detection task where the stimulus categories were signaled by an external cue, human subjects did not adjust the decision criterion to the levels used when each stimulus category was presented on its own (Gorea and Sagi, 2000).
evidence: This is a finding from cited prior work.

claim: Subjects behaved as if they assumed a common distribution of signals encompassing all stimulus conditions and applied a single decision criterion.
source: Instead, subjects behaved as if they assumed a common distribution of signals encompassing all stimulus conditions and applied a single decision criterion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of behavior from cited prior work.

claim: Subjects could perform above chance in a 2AFC experiment if they were trained to identify the higher volatility stimulus among a pair sharing the same motion strength.
source: Our volatility manipulation was more subtle than an explicit cue, but we do not doubt that our subjects could perform above chance in a 2AFC experiment if they were trained to identify the higher volatility stimulus among a pair sharing the same motion strength.
evidence: This is a speculation about what subjects could do under different conditions.

claim: When a mixture of different levels of volatility are presented in a sequence of otherwise similar events, subjects appear to combine trials of low and high volatility to form a single internal distribution with signed coherence as the only relevant dimension.
source: However, when a mixture of different levels of volatility are presented in a sequence of otherwise similar events (trials), subjects appear to combine trials of low and high volatility to form a single internal distribution with signed coherence as the only relevant dimension.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed behavior and model fits.

claim: Systems with multiple interacting units, like financial markets, sometimes give rise to 'leptokurtic' distributions.
source: Systems with multiple interacting units, like financial markets, sometimes give rise to 'leptokurtic' distributions, referred to as those where the probability of extreme events is larger than expected from normal distributions (Mandelbrot, 1997).
evidence: This is a statement about statistical distributions in complex systems, supported by a citation.

claim: A simple way of constructing leptokurtic distributions is by mixing Gaussian distributions that have the same mean but different variances.
source: A simple way of constructing leptokurtic distributions is by mixing Gaussian distributions that have the same mean but different variances, similar to our doubly stochastic (high volatility) stimulus.
evidence: This is a statement about statistical methods, related to the experimental design.

claim: When interpreting 'leptokurtic' noise, people appear to overreact to outliers.
source: When interpreting 'leptokurtic' noise, people appear to overreact to outliers.
evidence: This is a statement about human behavior in interpreting statistical distributions.

claim: When making stock investment decisions, people often misinterpret large fluctuations as evidence for a fundamental change in expected value.
source: For instance, when making stock investment decisions, people often misinterpret large fluctuations as evidence for a fundamental change in expected value (De Bondt and Thaler, 1990).
evidence: This is a finding from cited prior work in behavioral economics.

claim: Subjects interpreted the 'outliers' introduced by the doubly stochastic procedure as if they were caused by a higher coherence stimulus.
source: Similarly, our subjects interpreted the 'outliers' introduced by our doubly stochastic procedure (motion bursts of unlikely strength given the average motion strength of the trial) as if they were caused by a higher coherence stimulus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed behavior.

claim: Subjects behaved as if the noisy samples they acquired were generated by a mesokurtic distribution.
source: In this sense, they behaved as if the noisy samples they acquired were generated by a mesokurtic distribution (e.g., Gaussian).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed behavior.

claim: In the standard RDM stimulus, a dot that had appeared Δt ms ago is either displaced or replaced by a new dot at a random location within the stimulus aperture.
source: On each video frame, a dot that had appeared ∆t ms ago is either displaced (i.e., moved) or replaced by a new dot at a random location within the stimulus aperture.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus generation method.

claim: The determination of displacement versus replacement is in accordance with a flip of a biased coin, and the magnitude of this bias confers the motion strength.
source: The determination of displacement versus replacement is in accordance with a flip of a biased coin, and the magnitude of this bias confers the motion strength, which we refer to as a motion coherence (c).
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus generation method.

claim: In the standard RDM, the coherence, c, is fixed for the duration of an experimental trial.
source: In the standard RDM, the coherence, c, is fixed for the duration of an experimental trial (e.g., c = 0.13; Figure 2A, left, blue line).
evidence: This is a description of the standard stimulus condition.

claim: In the high volatility condition, the mean of c is fixed for the duration of a trial but the value of c varies randomly from video frame to video frame.
source: Here we introduce a second layer of variability, wherein the mean of c is fixed for the duration of a trial but the value of c varies randomly from video frame to video frame (Figure 2A, left, red line).
evidence: This is a description of the novel stimulus manipulation.

claim: The visual system blurs images over time, leading to the illusion that many more dots are present simultaneously than are actually displayed.
source: The visual system blurs these images over time, leading for example to the illusion that many more dots are present simultaneously than are actually displayed.
evidence: This is a statement about visual perception.

claim: The motion filter provides a reasonable approximation to the firing rates of direction selective neurons in the primate visual cortex.
source: The filter extracts a time-blurred motion signal that provides a reasonable approximation to the firing rates of direction selective neurons in the primate visual cortex (Britten et al., 1993; Rust et al., 2006; Hedges et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The mean motion energy is identical for low and high volatility stimuli, for all motion strengths.
source: A more systematic analysis of the motion energy, displayed in Figure 2B, reveals that the mean is identical for low and high volatility stimuli, for all motion strengths (upper panel), whereas the variance is larger for the high volatility stimuli (lower panel).
evidence: This is supported by the motion energy analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The variance of motion energy is larger for the high volatility stimuli.
source: A more systematic analysis of the motion energy, displayed in Figure 2B, reveals that the mean is identical for low and high volatility stimuli, for all motion strengths (upper panel), whereas the variance is larger for the high volatility stimuli (lower panel).
evidence: This is supported by the motion energy analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: For the low volatility condition, the motion energy variance is dominated by the variance in the number of coherently displaced dots, which obeys a binomial distribution.
source: For the low volatility condition (Figure 2B bottom, blue trace), the motion energy variance is dominated by the variance in the number of coherently displaced dots, which obeys a binomial distribution, hence the monotonic increase over the range of |c| = 0 to 0.5.
evidence: This is an explanation of the observed pattern in the motion energy variance.

claim: The effect of volatility on motion energy variance is strongest at the low coherences.
source: Note that the effect is strongest at the low coherences, where the distribution of c in the high volatility condition spans both positive and negative values.
evidence: This is an observation from the motion energy analysis.

claim: Neurons in areas MT/MST represent the momentary evidence used by monkeys to guide their choice, reaction time and confidence.
source: These neurons represent the momentary evidence used by monkeys to guide their choice, reaction time and confidence (Salzman et al., 1990; Celebrini and Newsome, 1995; Ditterich et al., 2003; Fetsch et al., 2014) in motion discrimination tasks.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The firing rate of MT neurons increases linearly, on average, as a function of motion strength in the neuron's preferred direction.
source: As previously shown (Britten et al., 1993), the firing rate of MT neurons increases linearly, on average, as a function of motion strength in the neuron's preferred direction (c > 0, Figure 2C, upper panel, blue trace).
evidence: This is supported by the neural data and cited prior work.

claim: The firing rate of MT neurons decreases linearly, but less steeply, as a function of motion strength in the anti-preferred direction.
source: The firing rate decreases linearly, but less steeply, as a function of motion strength in the anti-preferred direction (c < 0), giving rise to a bilinear function.
evidence: This is supported by the neural data.

claim: There is a subtle increase in firing rate at the low coherences under high volatility, which is explained by the rectification of neural responses.
source: These features are preserved under high volatility (red trace), but there is a subtle increase in firing rate at the low coherences, which is explained by the rectification of neural responses when the distribution of c spans positive and negative values (Figure 2C, inset).
evidence: This is supported by the neural data and an explanatory model.

claim: The variance of the neural response is known to scale approximately linearly with firing rate.
source: The variance of the neural response is known to scale approximately linearly with firing rate (Tolhurst et al., 1983; Vogels et al., 1989; Geisler and Albrecht, 1997; Shadlen and Newsome, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The high volatility condition adds to the variance in a manner that is exaggerated at the low motion strengths.
source: The high volatility condition adds to the variance in a manner that is exaggerated at the low motion strengths, consistent with the motion energy analysis above.
evidence: This is supported by the neural data analysis.

claim: The momentary evidence is the difference between the average firing rates from two pools of neurons with direction preferences for the two opposite directions.
source: We assume that the momentary evidence is the difference between the average firing rates from two pools of neurons with direction preferences for the two opposite directions (e.g., right-preferring minus left-preferring) (Shadlen et al., 1996; Ditterich et al., 2003; Hanks et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an assumption of the model, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The rectification is canceled by the subtraction of firing rates from opposing pools.
source: Notice that the rectification is now canceled by the subtraction.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of the difference variable.

claim: The beneficial effects of pooling saturate with modest number of neurons (e.g., 50–100).
source: An important implication of such correlation is that the beneficial effects of pooling saturate with modest number of neurons (e.g., 50–100; [Zohary et al., 1994; Shadlen et al., 1996]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The opposing pool is assumed to share the component of variance originating in the stimulus, albeit of opposite sign, so the variances add rather than cancel in the difference.
source: The opposing pool is assumed to share the component of variance originating in the stimulus, albeit of opposite sign, so the variances add rather than cancel in the difference.
evidence: This is an assumption about the structure of neural variability.

claim: The stimulus-independent component of shared variance should have the same sign in the two pools and thus cancel in the difference.
source: In contrast, the stimulus-independent component of shared variance (e.g., driven by fluctuations of arousal) should have the same sign in the two pools and thus cancel in the difference.
evidence: This is an assumption about the structure of neural variability.

claim: The volatility manipulation has negligible effects on the expectation of momentary evidence and more substantial effects on the variance, especially at weak motion strengths.
source: From these complementary analyses of stimulus and neural response, we conclude that the volatility manipulation has negligible effects on the expectation of momentary evidence and more substantial effects on the variance, especially at weak motion strengths.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the motion energy and neural data analyses.

claim: For both high and low volatility conditions, stronger motion led to faster and more accurate choices.
source: For both high and low volatility conditions, stronger motion led to faster and more accurate choices.
evidence: This is a basic finding from the behavioral data.

claim: The main effect of high volatility was to decrease RTs, particularly at the weakest motion strengths.
source: The main effect of high volatility was to decrease RTs, particularly at the weakest motion strengths (Figure 3B, bottom row, red).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the RT task, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The effect of volatility on RT was robust for all three human subjects and the monkey.
source: This effect was robust for all three human subjects and the monkey (Equation 16, all p<0.03, t-test, H0: β2=0).
evidence: This is supported by statistical tests on the behavioral data.

claim: The volatility manipulation affected the accuracy only subtly, and this was not statistically reliable for individual subjects in the RT task.
source: The manipulation affected the accuracy only subtly, and this was not statistically reliable for individual subjects in the RT task (Figure 3B, top row; for the four subjects: p=[0.35, 0.65, 0.2, 0.26], Equation 17, likelihood-ratio test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical tests on the behavioral data.

claim: There was a significant effect of volatility on accuracy when pooling data across subjects and including data from the confidence tasks.
source: However, there was a significant effect of volatility on accuracy when pooling data across subjects and including data from the confidence tasks described below (Equation 18, p<0.0005, likelihood ratio test, H0: β2=0; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical tests on the pooled behavioral data.

claim: The pattern of results in Figure 3B is consistent with the hypothesis that decisions are made when an accumulation of noisy evidence reaches a bound.
source: The pattern of results in Figure 3B is consistent with the hypothesis that decisions are made when an accumulation of noisy evidence reaches a bound.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data in relation to the theoretical model.

claim: The smooth curves in Figure 3B are fits of the bounded accumulation model to the data, where the variance of the momentary evidence is the only parameter allowed to change between conditions of high and low volatility.
source: Indeed, the smooth curves are fits of this model to the data, where the variance of the momentary evidence is the only parameter that we allowed to change between conditions of high and low volatility (see below).
evidence: This describes the modeling approach used to fit the data.

claim: The effect of increased volatility on RT is most apparent at motion strengths near zero because the volatility manipulation has a larger impact on variance of the motion energy at the weak motion strengths.
source: The effect of increased volatility on RT is most apparent at motion strengths near zero, for two reasons: (i) the volatility manipulation has a larger impact on variance of the motion energy at the weak motion strengths (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is an explanation of the observed pattern, supported by the motion energy analysis.

claim: The volatility manipulation mainly affects the weakest motion strengths where accuracy is already poor.
source: These considerations also help to reconcile the contrast between the striking effects of volatility on RT versus subtle effects on choice accuracy: the volatility manipulation mainly affects the weakest motion strengths where accuracy is already poor (but see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an explanation of the observed pattern of results.

claim: By increasing noise, the volatility manipulation accelerates the dispersion of the decision variable away from its expected value and nearer the termination bounds, hence faster RT.
source: The important point is that by increasing noise, the volatility manipulation accelerates the dispersion of the decision variable away from its expected value and nearer the termination bounds, hence faster RT.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism underlying the observed effects.

claim: Confidence can be formalized as the conditional probability of a correct choice given the state of the DV, which comprises the accumulated evidence and elapsed decision time.
source: In the framework of bounded evidence accumulation, it can be formalized as the conditional probability of a correct choice given the state of the DV, which comprises the accumulated evidence and elapsed decision time (Equation 5).
evidence: This is a description of how confidence is formalized in the theoretical framework.

claim: The mapping between DV and probability correct depends on the set of possible motion strengths, the two possible volatility conditions, and the amount of time that has elapsed in the trial.
source: It depends on the set of possible motion strengths (the prior distribution of c), the two possible volatility conditions, and the amount of time that has elapsed in the trial.
evidence: This is a description of the factors that determine the mapping.

claim: The subject has implicit knowledge of the mapping between DV and probability correct, and does not adjust it when a low or high volatility stimulus is shown.
source: We assume the subject has implicit knowledge of this mapping, and does not adjust it when a low or high volatility stimulus is shown.
evidence: This is an assumption of the modeling approach.

claim: The assumption that subjects do not adjust the mapping is justified because volatility levels were randomly interleaved and not cued or even mentioned to the subjects.
source: The latter seems justified because volatility levels were randomly interleaved and not cued or even mentioned to the subjects (we evaluate this assumption, below, in several alternative models).
evidence: This is a justification for the modeling assumption, based on the experimental design.

claim: Increased volatility should affect confidence because it mimics an increase in the diffusion rate.
source: Increased volatility should affect confidence because it mimics an increase in the diffusion rate.
evidence: This is a prediction from the theoretical framework.

claim: At low coherences, the main effect of volatility on the DV is to accelerate its exodus away from neutral to more extreme values.
source: At low coherences in particular, its main effect on the DV is to accelerate its exodus away from neutral (probability correct = 0.5) to more extreme values.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism underlying the predicted effect on confidence.

claim: Volatility would increase confidence at low coherences, for the same reason that it speeds the RT.
source: Therefore, we predicted that volatility would increase confidence at low coherences, for the same reason that it speeds the RT.
evidence: This is a prediction from the theoretical framework.

claim: The monkey made rational use of the sure bet, opting out more often for weaker motion.
source: In both low and high volatility conditions, the monkey made rational use of the sure bet, opting out more often for weaker motion (Equation 19, p<10–6, logistic regression, likelihood-ratio test; Figure 4B)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: The monkey made rational use of the sure bet, opting out more often for briefer stimuli.
source: In both low and high volatility conditions, the monkey made rational use of the sure bet, opting out more often for weaker motion (Equation 19, p<10–6, logistic regression, likelihood-ratio test; Figure 4B) and for briefer stimuli (Equation 19, p<10–6, logistic regression; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: When the sure bet was offered but waived, choice accuracy was higher than when the sure bet was not offered.
source: When the sure bet was offered but waived, choice accuracy was higher than when the sure bet was not offered (Equation 20, p<10–6, logistic regression; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: The monkey was more likely to opt out of rendering its decision when the answer was more likely to be wrong.
source: This indicates that the monkey was more likely to opt out of rendering its decision when the answer was more likely to be wrong.
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral data.

claim: The decision to accept or waive the sure bet is based on the state of the evidence on the trial and not a general propensity associated with each motion strength.
source: It implies that the decision to accept or waive the sure bet is based on the state of the evidence on the trial and not a general propensity associated with each motion strength (Kiani and Shadlen, 2009).
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral data, supported by a citation.

claim: The proportion of trials the monkey decided to waive the sure-bet option was greater on the high volatility trials.
source: As shown in Figure 4B (lower panel), the proportion of trials the monkey decided to waive the sure-bet option (deciding instead for a riskier direction choice) was greater on the high volatility trials (Equation 19, p<10–6, likelihood-ratio test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: High volatility increased the monkey's confidence despite a negligible effect on accuracy.
source: Thus, high volatility increased the monkey's confidence, and did so despite a negligible effect on accuracy (Figure 4B, upper).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the PDW task.

claim: Like its effect on RT, volatility affected PDW mainly when the motion was weak.
source: Further, like its effect on RT, volatility affected PDW mainly when the motion was weak (Figure 4B, lower).
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral data.

claim: Human subjects were more confident for high coherence stimuli.
source: Naturally, subjects were more confident for high coherence stimuli (Equation 21, p<10–6, t-test; Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: Human subjects reported higher confidence for the high volatility stimuli, and the effect was most apparent for the low coherence stimuli.
source: They also reported higher confidence for the high volatility stimuli, and the effect was most apparent for the low coherence stimuli (Equation 21, p<0.0004, t-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: A single bounded accumulation model can account for the combined effect of motion strength and volatility on choice, accuracy and RT.
source: Now we show how a single bounded accumulation model can account for the combined effect of motion strength and volatility on choice, accuracy and RT.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model fits presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the model, choice, RT and confidence result from the accumulation of noisy momentary evidence as a function of time, until the integral of the evidence reaches one of two bounds, or until the stimulus is curtailed.
source: In the model, choice, RT and confidence result from the accumulation of noisy momentary evidence as a function of time, until the integral of the evidence (the decision variable, DV) reaches one of two bounds, or for the PDW and confidence tasks, until the stimulus is curtailed.
evidence: This is a description of the model.

claim: The DV is updated at each time step by the addition of a constant, proportional to motion strength, plus a draw from a zero-mean Gaussian distribution.
source: The DV is updated at each time step by the addition of a constant, proportional to motion strength, plus a draw from a zero-mean Gaussian distribution.
evidence: This is a description of the model.

claim: The partial rectification implies that the variance of the difference should increase as a function of motion strength.
source: However, the partial rectification (Figure 2C) implies that the variance of the difference should increase as a function of motion strength.
evidence: This is an inference from the neural data.

claim: The difference in noise between volatility conditions is larger at 0% coherence and decays gradually for stronger motion.
source: These analyses showed that (i) the variance of the momentary evidence increases with motion strength, and (ii) the difference in noise between volatility conditions is larger at 0% coherence and decays gradually for stronger motion.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the motion energy and neural analyses.

claim: The framework can explain confidence if we assume that the brain has implicit knowledge of the state of the accumulated evidence, the elapsed deliberation time, and the mapping of time and evidence to the probability of making a correct choice.
source: The framework can explain confidence if we assume that the brain has implicit knowledge of (i) the state of the accumulated evidence, (ii) the elapsed deliberation time, and (iii) the mapping of time and evidence to the probability of making a correct choice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a description of the assumptions underlying the confidence model.

claim: Time matters because the same level of accumulated evidence is associated with lower levels of accuracy if the evidence was accrued over longer periods of time.
source: Time matters because the same level of accumulated evidence is associated with lower levels of accuracy if the evidence was accrued over longer periods of time (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an explanation of why time is important in the confidence model.

claim: In the human confidence task, probability correct is transformed into a confidence rating through a monotonic transformation.
source: In the human confidence task, probability correct is transformed into a confidence rating through a monotonic transformation (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of how the model implements the confidence rating task.

claim: The confidence curves in Figure 5B can be considered predictions of the model.
source: All other parameters were taken from the RT task, performed by the same participants. Therefore, the confidence curves in Figure 5B can be considered predictions of the model.
evidence: This is a statement about the modeling approach.

claim: The predictions capture the trend well, supporting the notion that time and accumulated evidence are the main determinants of confidence in a perceptual choice.
source: These predictions capture the trend well, supporting the notion that time and accumulated evidence are the main determinants of confidence in a perceptual choice, even when noise is under experimental control.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model predictions in relation to the data.

claim: The overall quality of the fits indicates that the influence of motion strength and volatility on choice, reaction time and confidence can be explained by a common mechanism of bounded evidence accumulation.
source: The overall quality of the fits—across all tasks and both species—indicates that the influence of motion strength and volatility on choice, reaction time and confidence can be explained by a common mechanism of bounded evidence accumulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: The 'two map' model produces visibly worse fits than the model that relies on a common map, despite having the same number of parameters.
source: When fit to data, this two-map model produces visibly worse fits than the model that relies on a common map, despite having the same number of parameters (Figure 6B; ∆BIC = 252.4 favoring the common-map model; see Table 2 for parameter fits).
evidence: This is supported by the model comparison analysis.

claim: For the second two-map model, the rate estimated from the best fit is exceedingly slow.
source: Interestingly, the rate estimated from the best fit is exceedingly slow. For example, after 1 s of viewing, the weight assigned to the appropriate volatility map is just 1%.
evidence: This is a result from fitting the alternative model.

claim: The confidence is dominated by the common mapping, consistent with the assumption.
source: In other words, the confidence is dominated by the common mapping, consistent with our assumption.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model fitting results.

claim: The model that allows different bound heights for the two volatility conditions in the PDW task was inferior to the simpler common-map model.
source: This model was also inferior to the simpler common-map model (∆BIC = 127; see Table 2 for parameter fits).
evidence: This is supported by the model comparison analysis.

claim: The model for the RT task that allowed the bounds to be different for the two volatility conditions led to a marginal increase in the likelihoods, but not enough to justify the addition of the extra parameter.
source: We also fit a model for the RT task that allowed the bounds to be different for the two volatility conditions. This led to a marginal increase in the likelihoods, but not enough to justify the addition of the extra parameter (∆BIC = [29.4, 7.7, 27.3, 12.1] for the four subjects; Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by the model comparison analysis.

claim: The analyses of alternative models support the assumption that subjects applied a common mapping and decision strategy on trials of low and high volatility.
source: These analyses of alternative models support our assumption that subjects applied a common mapping and decision strategy on trials of low and high volatility.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model comparison analyses.

claim: The common mapping assumption is likely a consequence of the particular volatility manipulation and task designs employed.
source: We do not believe this holds generally but is likely a consequence of the particular volatility manipulation and task designs we employed.
evidence: This is a speculation about the generality of the findings.

claim: The normative strategy for several model tasks would apply different bounds and mappings to the two volatility conditions.
source: Indeed, the normative strategy for several model tasks, which approximate those in our study, would apply different bounds and mappings to the two volatility conditions (see Appendix).
evidence: This is a statement about normative models, with reference to the Appendix.

claim: The full normative solution for the tasks used is not known.
source: The full normative solution for the tasks we used is not known.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current theoretical understanding.

claim: It is not known if subjects performed suboptimally or if they were simply unable to identify the volatility conditions without adding additional costs.
source: Hence, we do not know if our subjects performed suboptimally or if they were simply unable to identify the volatility conditions without adding additional costs (e.g., effort and/or time).
evidence: This is a statement about the uncertainty in interpreting the results.

claim: Three interleaved sets of dots were drawn in successive frames at a monitor refresh rate of 75 Hz.
source: Briefly, three interleaved sets of dots were drawn in successive frames (monitor refresh rate: 75 Hz).
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus generation method.

claim: When a dot disappeared, it was redrawn 40 ms later either at a random location in the stimulus aperture or displaced in the direction of motion.
source: When a dot disappeared, it was redrawn 40 ms later (i.e., 3 video frames) either at a random location in the stimulus aperture or displaced in the direction of motion.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus generation method.

claim: Three human participants completed 6631 trials in the RT task.
source: Three human participants completed 6631 trials (subject S1: 2490 trials; S2: 2070; S3: 2071), and one macaque (monkey W) completed 14,137 trials.
evidence: This is a description of the sample size.

claim: One macaque (monkey W) completed 14,137 trials in the RT task.
source: Three human participants completed 6631 trials (subject S1: 2490 trials; S2: 2070; S3: 2071), and one macaque (monkey W) completed 14,137 trials.
evidence: This is a description of the sample size.

claim: Dot density was 16.7 dots/deg2/s, and the displacement of the coherent dots was consistent with apparent motion of 5 deg/sec.
source: Dot density was 16.7 dots/deg2/s, and the displacement of the coherent dots was consistent with apparent motion of 5 deg/sec.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus parameters.

claim: A minimum time of 950 ms was imposed from dot onset to reward delivery for the monkey in order to discourage fast guessing.
source: For the monkey, a minimum time of 950 ms was imposed from dot onset to reward delivery (e.g., Hanks et al., 2011) in order to discourage fast guessing.
evidence: This is a description of the task design, supported by a citation.

claim: Trials employing 0% coherence motion were deemed correct with probability ½.
source: Trials employing 0% coherence motion were deemed correct with probability ½.
evidence: This is a description of the task design.

claim: Monkey D performed a total of 65,751 behavioral trials in the PDW task.
source: The monkey performed a total of 65,751 behavioral trials, a subset of which (44,334 trials) were accompanied by neurophysiological recordings.
evidence: This is a description of the sample size.

claim: A subset of 44,334 trials in the PDW task were accompanied by neurophysiological recordings.
source: The monkey performed a total of 65,751 behavioral trials, a subset of which (44,334 trials) were accompanied by neurophysiological recordings.
evidence: This is a description of the sample size.

claim: By convention, positive motion coherences correspond to the preferred direction of motion of the recorded neurons.
source: By convention, positive motion coherences correspond to the preferred direction of motion of the recorded neurons.
evidence: This is a description of the convention used in the analysis.

claim: The same three observers that performed the reaction time task participated in the human confidence task.
source: The same three observers that performed the reaction time task participated in this second experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In the human confidence task, the RDM was displayed for a fixed 200 ms on each trial.
source: The RDM (low or high volatility, randomly interleaved) was displayed for a fixed 200 ms on each trial, after which they reported the perceived direction of motion (left or right) and the confidence in their decision.
evidence: This is a description of the task design.

claim: Subjects were allowed to adjust their gaze to the desired level before finalizing their combined choice and confidence report.
source: They were allowed to adjust their gaze to the desired level before finalizing their combined choice and confidence report (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a description of the task design.

claim: All animal procedures complied with guidelines from the National Institutes of Health and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Columbia University.
source: All animal procedures complied with guidelines from the National Institutes of Health and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Columbia University.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: Multi- and single-unit recordings were made with tungsten electrodes (1–2 MΩ, FHC).
source: Multi- (MU) and single-unit (SU) recordings were made with tungsten electrodes (1–2 MΩ, FHC).
evidence: This is a description of the recording methods.

claim: Areas MT and MST were identified using structural MRI scans and standard physiological criteria.
source: Areas MT (n = 13 SU and 9 MU sites) and MST (n = 13 SU, 12 MU) were identified using structural MRI scans and standard physiological criteria.
evidence: This is a description of the recording methods.

claim: No substantial differences were observed between MT and MST in the main results, and therefore the data were pooled.
source: We did not observe substantial differences between the two areas in the main results (Figure 2) and therefore pooled the data for all analyses.
evidence: This is a statement about the data analysis approach.

claim: The sample size is too small to rule out subtle differences between MT and MST.
source: However, the sample size is too small to rule out subtle differences between areas.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the data.

claim: The variance in the high volatility condition was constrained to be monotonically increasing.
source: We constrained the variance in the high volatility condition to be monotonically increasing.
evidence: This is a description of a modeling constraint.

claim: The difference between the reaction time and the decision time is the non-decision latency, assumed to reflect sensory and motor delays unrelated to motion strength or volatility.
source: The difference between the reaction time and the decision time is the non-decision latency, assumed to reflect sensory and motor delays unrelated to motion strength or volatility.
evidence: This is a description of a model component.

claim: In the PDW task, bounds merely curtail the expected improvement in accuracy on longer duration stimuli.
source: This is not surprising because in the PDW task, stimulus duration is controlled by the experimenter, and bounds merely curtail the expected improvement in accuracy on longer duration stimuli.
evidence: This is an explanation of why a particular model feature is not important for the PDW task.

claim: In the human confidence experiment, the presence of bounds did not improve the quality of the fits.
source: In the human confidence task, the presence of bounds did not improve the quality of the fits.
evidence: This is a result from the model fitting.

claim: Subjects used all the stimulus information to inform their choices in the human confidence task, presumably because the stimulus duration was only 0.2 s.
source: This implies that subjects used all the stimulus information to inform their choices, presumably because the stimulus duration was only 0.2 s.
evidence: This is an inference from the model fitting results.

claim: The area under the ROC curve for classifying volatility from motion energy was 0.895.
source: The area under the ROC curve was 0.895, indicating that there is information in the stimulus to reliably estimate the volatility condition of each trial, even for the brief stimulus presentations used in the PDW task.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of motion energy.

claim: The calculation of volatility classification is not put forward as a plausible model for inferring volatility, but merely serves to document that information is present in the stimuli.
source: To be clear, we do not put forward this calculation as a plausible model for inferring volatility. It merely serves to document that information is present in the stimuli to render a categorization possible.
evidence: This is a clarification about the purpose of the analysis.

claim: Spike counts were restricted to trials where the motion stimulus was presented for at least 150 ms to avoid artifacts produced by the response to the offset of the RDM stimulus.
source: To avoid artifacts produced by the response to the offset of the RDM stimulus, we restricted this analysis to trials where the motion stimulus was presented for at least 150 ms.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method.

claim: Findings from neurophysiology and computational modeling suggest that the momentary evidence is proportional to the difference of firing rates between pools of neurons with opposite direction preferences.
source: Findings from neurophysiology (Ditterich et al., 2003) and computational modeling (Mazurek et al., 2003) suggest that the momentary evidence is proportional to the difference of firing rates between pools of neurons with opposite direction preferences (e.g., right-preferring minus left-preferring).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: For the analyses depicted in Figure 7, spike times were extracted from each trial up to 50 ms after motion offset and then smoothed with a centered boxcar filter with a 30 ms width.
source: For the analyses depicted in Figure 7, we extracted the spike times from each trial up to 50 ms after motion offset and then smoothed the spike counts with a centered boxcar filter with a 30 ms width.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method.

claim: The latencies in Figure 7B were estimated with a curve fitting procedure based on the CUSUM method.
source: The latencies in Figure 7B were estimated with a curve fitting procedure based on the CUSUM method (Ellaway, 1978).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method, supported by a citation.

claim: Standard errors of the latency estimates were derived with a bootstrapping procedure (N = 1000).
source: Standard errors of the latency estimates were derived with a bootstrapping procedure (N = 1000).
evidence: This is a description of the statistical method.
